  • The Tyburn Tree (The Triple Tree): A permanent wooden structure consisting of three heavy horizontal oak beams supported on three timber legs. Eight condemned felons could be tied to each beam, allowing twenty-four people to hang in a single drop.
  • The Nubbing Cheat: The hanging gallows or the noose itself. To be 'nubbed' was to be hanged by the neck.
  • Padding-Fair: Execution day at Tyburn. A riotous public holiday where thousands of Londoners drank gin, ate roasted nuts, and cheered or jeered as the open horse carts rolled past bearing the condemned prisoners sitting on their own coffins.

The Fatal Drop and 'The Caper'

Before the invention of the mechanical trapdoor drop in 1783, hanging was slow suffocation. The noose was tied to the crossbeam while the felon stood in an open cart. The executioner whipped the horses, the cart rolled away, and the felon swung in the air, slowly strangling to death over 10 to 20 minutes—a horrific agonal spasm termed by the crowd **'Dancing the Tyburn Jig'**.
fiction_tips: • The Nosegay on the Cart: Condemned highwaymen dressed in their finest silk coats on their ride to Tyburn, wearing a nosegay of flowers pinned to their lapels, stopping at the Bowl Inn in St. Giles for a final free tankard of sack with the crowd cheering them like rock stars. • Pulling on the Legs: Crucial authentic detail: friends and family of the hanging felon would rush forward beneath the gallows, grab the swinging felon's boots, and pull downward with all their weight to snap the neck and end the agonizing suffocation quickly. • The Resurrection Men: Describe the violent fistfights beneath the gallows between the felon's friends (trying to secure the corpse for burial) and surgeons' body-snatchers (trying to steal the corpse for anatomical dissection).

title: Regency London Rookeries and Flash Houses: St. Giles and The Holy Land
summary: The geography of Regency London's criminal underworld from Grose's 1811 lexicon: the St. Giles Rookery ('The Holy Land'), debtor sanctuaries, and Flash Houses.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.The Rookeries: Densely packed urban slums with interconnected cellar labyrinths where constables and bailiffs feared to enter.
quick_facts.The Holy Land (St. Giles): The most notorious rookery in London; crowded with Irish laborers, thieves, gin-shops, and beggars.
quick_facts.Flash House: A public house or gin tavern licensed as a legitimate tavern, but serving as an open headquarters and fencing depot for thieves.
quick_facts.Sanctuaries (The Mint & Fleet): Ancient privileged zones where civil debt bailiffs could not legally arrest debtors without military support.

content:
The Labyrinths of Regency Vice

In 1811, London was the largest and wealthiest metropolis on the globe, yet beneath the neoclassical marble facades of Mayfair and Regent Street lay terrifying urban slums termed **Rookeries**—lawless warrens of decaying timber tenements where the King's writ did not run.

The Architecture of the St. Giles Rookery

Situated between modern-day Oxford Street and Covent Garden, the St. Giles Rookery (mockingly known as **The Holy Land**) was an impenetrable criminal sanctuary:

  • Interconnected Warrens: Tenements had cellars knocked together into continuous subterranean tunnels, and rooftops fitted with loose planks that could be laid across narrow alleys to flee pursuit across roof ridges. A thief chased by Bow Street Runners could run into a front door and emerge three streets away in five minutes.
  • Open Sewage and Gin: Raw sewage ran down central stone gutters; entire families rented 'tuppenny rope' beds (sleeping leaning over a horizontal rope strung across a cellar, unhooked at 6 AM).

The Flash House Culture

Thieves did not operate in damp shadows; they drank openly in **Flash Houses**—taverns where young pickpockets, dashing highwaymen, prostitute doxies, and corrupt Bow Street Runners drank gin together. The landlord acted as the primary **Fence** (receiver of stolen goods), buying pocketbooks, melting silver spoons in a back kitchen crucible, and tipping off officers when a rogue's reward climbed high enough to make his arrest profitable.
fiction_tips: • The Tuppenny Hang: Describe a sleeping cellar in the rookery: sixty shivering beggars sitting on wooden benches, leaning forward with their arms crossed over a long taut clothesline, paying two pennies for the right to sleep hanging over the rope. • The Flash Dialect: Flash language is faster, punchier, and more ironic than 17th-century cant: characters speak of 'rolling in the flash' and 'knowing the game.' • The Smells of St. Giles: St. Giles smells of boiled cabbage, rancid mutton fat, unwashed damp wool, cheap gin, and unslaked lime thrown over open cesspools.

title: Regency Pugilism and The Fancy: Milling, Fibbing, and The Sweet Science
summary: The colorful dialect of Regency bare-knuckle prizefighting from Grose: The Fancy enthusiasts, Broughton's rules, milling, fibbing, and tapping claret.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.The Fancy: The aristocratic sporting subculture (noblemen, dandies, poets like Lord Byron) obsessed with bare-knuckle prize-fighting.
quick_facts.Milling (Fighting): To beat, strike, or fight ('A mill' = a boxing match; 'A milling cove' = a prizefighter).
quick_facts.Fibbing (Close Quarters): Holding an opponent's head in chancery (headlock) with one arm while delivering rapid, repetitive rabbit punches to the ribs with the other.
quick_facts.Tapping the Claret: Striking the opponent's nose or mouth so hard that dark red arterial blood flows like claret wine.

content:
The Golden Age of Bare Knuckles

In Regency England, bare-knuckle boxing—'The Sweet Science'—was an illegal yet wildly popular national obsession. Dukes, earls, and the Prince Regent himself rode in barouches side-by-side with tavern butchers and pickpockets to watch forty-round bloody contests fought in muddy fields outside London jurisdiction under **Broughton's Rules** (1743).

The Lexicon of the Prizering

  • The Mill: The fight itself. To 'mill' someone was to batter them with fists. A 'milling match' went on until one man was knocked unconscious or could not 'come up to the scratch' (the chalk line in the center of the ring) within 30 seconds.
  • In Chancery: Getting an opponent's neck tucked under your left armpit in a tight headlock. While locked in chancery, the victim's head cannot move, allowing the fighter to **fib** his ribs and kidneys with short, violent, piston-like right-hand blows.
  • The Breadbasket: The stomach / solar plexus. A crushing blow to the breadbasket knocked all wind from the lungs, dropping the strongest champion.
  • Drawing the Cork / Tapping the Claret: Punching the bridge of the nose or lips, unleashing a fountain of dark red blood (claret).
  • The Daylights / Peepers: The eyes. To 'darken his daylights' meant swelling both eyelids completely shut with bare-knuckle bruising so the fighter was blind.
  • The Cross-Buttock: Under early rules, wrestling was completely legal; a cross-buttock throw hip-tossed the opponent violently onto the turf, landing on top of his ribs with full body weight.
fiction_tips: • The Bare-Knuckle Reality: Without boxing gloves, fighters could not throw heavy head punches without breaking their own metacarpal bones. Bare-knuckle fighters aimed predominantly at the ribs, chest, neck, and eyes, using palm heels and hammer fists. • The Ringside Roar: Describe the aristocratic Fancy: wealthy dandies in multi-caped coats and beaver top hats shouting bets with thick handfuls of bank notes, drinking hot spiced gin while two battered, swollen-faced men bleed into the sawdust. • The Sponge and Brandy: Between 30-second rounds, seconds washed the fighter's face with vinegar sponges, blew brandy into their eyes to clear swelling, and massaged cramped thighs.

title: Gambling Hells and Sharpers' Cant: Cogging Dice, Greeks, and Pigeons
summary: The predatory underworld of Regency gambling dens: loaded 'doctors' dice, the palm cog, card sharps (Greeks), and plucking a wealthy pigeon.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.Gambling Hells: Illicit high-stakes gaming clubs in London (e.g. St. James's) equipped with barred iron doors and secret escape trapdoors.
quick_facts.A Greek: A professional cheat or card sharper who makes his living fleecing naive players with sleight-of-hand.
quick_facts.A Pigeon: A young, wealthy, foolish heir just inherited a country estate, ripe for swindling by the Greeks ('Plucking the Pigeon').
quick_facts.The Doctors (Loaded Dice): Dice drilled out, weighted with liquid mercury or lead on one side, and re-capped so specific numbers roll with statistical certainty.
quick_facts.Cogging: The manual sleight-of-hand skill of sliding or holding one die motionless against the fingers while tossing the other.

content:
The Swindling Salons of St. James's

Gambling was the ruinous vice of Georgian and Regency aristocracy. Fortunes of fifty thousand pounds, ancestral estates, and whole counties changed hands in a single night over games of **Hazard** (dice) and **Macao / Faro** (cards). Where fortunes flowed, the **Sharpers** and **Greeks** gathered to orchestrate mathematical and mechanical theft.

The Arsenal of the Dice Sharp

  • Doctors (Loaded Dice): High-precision false dice. A hole is drilled through a pip, a drop of heavy mercury is placed in a tiny hollow chamber, and sealed with bone dust. The die lands with the heavy side down 70% of the time, rolling high or low numbers on demand.
  • Brimmers and Flats: Dice cut slightly out of square (rectangular rather than cubic), making certain numbers roll more frequently because the larger surface area tends to settle on the table.
  • Cogging the Dice: The master sharper does not need loaded dice. He places one die securely between his ring finger and palm, rattles the other die noisily inside the leather dice-box, and tosses: one die rolls naturally, while the second die is slid smoothly onto the baize cloth showing the exact face the sharper desires.

Plucking the Pigeon

The universal con: a team of smooth, elegantly dressed Greeks befriends a young country squire (**the Pigeon**) who has just inherited his father's rent-rolls. They praise his wit, ply him with vintage champagne, allow him to win two hundred guineas on the first two nights, and on the third night, introduce loaded dice, stripping the Pigeon of his horses, his town house, and his ancestral acres before sunrise.
fiction_tips: • The Dice Box Sound: Dice boxes were lined with ribbed horn or concentric metal rings to make the rattle loud; a sharp dealer uses a smooth leather box so he can slide dice out without tumbling. • The Armed Lookout: High-stakes gambling hells kept an armed 'Ruffian' behind double iron doors with a peephole, ready to dump dice into an open fireplace when the Bow Street bailiffs battered the door. • The Suicide at Dawn: Describe the grim aftermath of the hells: ruined young aristocrats stumbling out into the morning fog on the way to the Serpentine lake with an empty purse and an unloaded horse pistol.

title: Gentlemen of the Road: The High Toby, Low Toby, and Barking Irons
summary: Mounted highwaymen vs brutal pedestrian footpads from Grose's dictionary: the High Toby code, flintlock barking irons, prancing steeds, and road ambushes.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.The High Toby: The mounted highwayman; considered an aristocrat among criminals; rode blooded thoroughbreds, wore silk masks and cloaks.
quick_facts.The Low Toby: The desperate footpad; unmounted pedestrian robber who lurked in muddy ditches to bludgeon travelers with leaded cudgels.
quick_facts.Barking Irons: Flintlock horse pistols (named for the loud barking snap and concussive muzzle report).
quick_facts.Prancer: A horse ('To prance' = to ride on the highway).
quick_facts.The Stand and Deliver: The traditional challenge to coaches: 'Stand and deliver your money or your life!'

content:
The Aristocrats and Monsters of the King's Highway

Before paved turnpikes and mounted police patrols, the dark unlit heaths surrounding London (Hounslow Heath, Finchley Common, Blackheath) were gauntlets of terror for traveling coaches. Grose's 1811 dictionary draws a sharp, unforgiving line between the mounted **High Toby** and the murderous **Low Toby**.

The High Toby (The Highwayman)

Mounted on a fast thoroughbred mare, the High Toby gentleman was romanticized in broadside ballads. He dressed in gentleman's riding boots, a multi-caped beaver coat, and wore a black crape mask. He stopped the post-chaise at pistol point, bowed to the ladies, demanded gold watches and purses, and rarely resorted to murder unless fired upon by the coachman's blunderbuss.

The Low Toby (The Footpad)

The footpad possessed zero romance. Penniless, filthy, and operating on foot in bands of three, footpads hid in ditches along muddy crossroads. They did not shout polite commands; they threw an iron crowbar into the coach wheel spokes, dragged the driver from the box, beat the passengers senseless with lead-filled cudgels (**bludgeons**), stripped victims naked in the freezing mud, and cut throats to eliminate witnesses.

The Weapons: Barking Irons and Blunderbusses

  • Barking Irons: Large, smoothbore flintlock pistols firing a massive 0.65-caliber lead ball. Carried in leather pommel holsters on either side of the horse's saddle.
  • The Guard's Blunderbuss: The mail coach guard rode atop the boot armed with a brass-barreled blunderbuss loaded with a handful of lead musket balls and buckshot, designed to sweep the road in front of the horses with a devastating cone of fire.
fiction_tips: • The Wet Priming Pan: In a highway robbery scene, remember flintlock mechanics: if it is raining, water seeping into the open pan can cause a 'flash in the pan' (powder burns without igniting the main charge) or completely misfire, leaving the highwayman with an empty club. • The Hounslow Gibbet: Highwaymen who were caught and executed at Tyburn were not buried; their corpses were dipped in boiling pitch (tar), wrapped in iron chains (**hung in chains**), and suspended from tall wooden gibbets on Hounslow Heath to rot in the wind as a grisly warning to approaching travelers. • The Hostler Informer: Highwaymen got their intelligence from crooked stable boys (hostlers) at roadside coaching inns, who checked how heavily travelers' saddlebags thumped and tipped off the road agent for a cut of the gold.

title: Taverns, Gin Palaces, and Tippling Slang: Blue Ruin and Heavy Wet
summary: The vivid drinking and intoxication lexicon of Georgian England: Blue Ruin (lethal gin), Flash of Lightning, Heavy Wet, and the ranks of drunkenness.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.Blue Ruin / Madame Geneva: Cheap, adulterated commercial gin; distilled with oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) and turpentine; ruined entire working-class districts.
quick_facts.Heavy Wet: Porter or strong dark stout ale; favored by draymen and pugilists for stamina.
quick_facts.Flash of Lightning: A single dram (shot) of raw spirits swallowed neat at the bar.
quick_facts.Lushington: A dedicated drunkard ('Lush' = liquor; 'To be lushing' = to drink heavily).
quick_facts.Yard of Flannel: A pint of warm home-brewed ale beaten with raw egg, grated ginger, nutmeg, and a dash of gin.

content:
The Gin Epidemic of Georgian London

During the 18th and early 19th centuries, London was consumed by the 'Gin Craze.' Unregulated street distilleries churned out millions of gallons of cheap, fiery liquor that cost a penny a bowl. Hogarth's famous engraving *Gin Lane* captured the societal collapse, while Captain Grose's dictionary catalogued the extraordinary linguistic variety used by citizens to describe intoxication.

The Drinks of the Street

  • Blue Ruin: The street name for cheap gin, so called because of its pale bluish tint (from turpentine and sulfuric acid adulterants) and the total domestic ruin it brought to families. Also affectionately personified as **Madame Geneva** or **Mother's Milk**.
  • Heavy Wet: Dark, heavy, malty London Porter beer. Considered healthy, nourishing, and respectable compared to the degenerate madness of gin.
  • Strip-Me-Naked: Another cant name for gin, because impoverished addicts pawned their coats, shirts, and bedsheets to buy another dram.
  • Dog's Nose: A popular tavern mixture: a pint of cold porter spiced with brown sugar, nutmeg, and an added glass of gin.

The Degrees of Drunkenness

Grose meticulously classifies the linguistic spectrum of inebriation:

  1. Muzzy: Slightly tipsy; confused, blinking like an owl.
  2. Elevated: High-spirited, talkative, singing in the parlor.
  3. Groggy: Staggering, legs rubbery (derived from naval grog).
  4. Disguised: So thoroughly drunk that normal character is unrecognizable.
  5. Sewed Up: Passed out cold on the taproom sawdust floor, completely helpless.
fiction_tips: • The Gin Shop Atmosphere: Describe an authentic early gin shop: no chairs or tables (which encourage lingering); just a narrow zinc bar counter, giant wooden barrels painted gold with brass spigots, sawdust on the floor to soak up vomit, and gaslights glaring through toxic fumes. • The Adulteration Reality: Street gin was rarely pure grain alcohol; cheap distillers cut it with **oil of turpentine, sulfuric acid, and alum** to give it a sharp, fiery bite, which literally dissolved the stomach linings of chronic drinkers. • Tavern Slang Dialogue: Use Grose's idioms naturally: 'Come, landlord, draw us another pint of heavy wet and a flash of lightning to warm the blood!'

title: Georgian Naval Slang: Jack Tar, Grog, Bilboes, and Banyan Days
summary: The colloquial dialect of Royal Navy sailors between the decks from Grose's dictionary: Jack Tar idiom, the origin of Grog, bilboes, and Holy Ground.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.Jack Tar: The universal nickname for an English sailor; derived from their tar-smeared canvas jackets, trousers, and hats.
quick_facts.Grog (Admiral Vernon 1740): Rum watered down with 3 parts water + lime juice; named after Vernon's grogram cloak ('Old Grog').
quick_facts.Bilboes: Long iron bars with sliding shackles bolted to the deck, used to lock mutinous sailors by the ankles.
quick_facts.Banyan Day: A day when no meat was issued to the ship's crew (usually cheese, pease pudding, and bread only; derived from Hindu banyans who eat no meat).

content:
The Unique Language of the Wooden World

Isolated aboard wooden ships for three-year voyages across global oceans, the sailors of the Royal Navy developed a specialized dialect that was virtually incomprehensible to civilian landsmen. Captain Grose recorded this salty, irreverent argot at the height of the Napoleonic Wars.

The Sailor's Lexicon

  • Jack Tar: The common seaman. Real sailors wore wide trousers and short canvas jackets heavily coated in black Stockholm tar to make them waterproof against ocean spray.
  • The Bilboes: The naval punishment lock. A heavy horizontal iron bar bolted to the deck; the prisoner's legs were placed into iron U-shackles that locked onto the bar. If the ship rolled in a gale, the iron shackles sheared the skin from the prisoner's shins.
  • Slop Chest: The ship's store of standardized clothing (slops—canvas trousers, wool shirts, stockings) issued by the purser and deducted from the sailor's pay.
  • Purser's Grin: A hypocritical, false, sneering smile; derived from the purser (the ship's business officer), who was universally suspected by sailors of cheating them out of meat, cheese, and rum rations.
  • Holy Ground: The red-light tavern and brothel district in port cities (such as Portsmouth Point), so named because sailors swore it was 'paradise on earth.'
  • Fiddler's Green: The mythical paradise reserved exclusively for sailors who served fifty years before the mast, complete with perpetual grog and zero officers.
fiction_tips: • Banyan Day Grumbling: Show the mess deck grumbling on a Banyan Day: sailors picking through cold, rock-hard pease pudding and moldy cheese, tapping hardtack ship biscuits against the wooden mess table to knock out the crawling black weevil grubs before taking a bite. • The Grog Tub Ritual: Describe the noon grog ceremony: the brass-bound oak grog tub inscribed with golden letters: 'THE KING, GOD BLESS HIM', with seamen lining up with tin cups under the watchful eye of the Royal Marine sentry. • Landlubber Contempt: Jack Tars looked upon anyone who lived on land with pure pity and disdain, referring to them as 'shore-crawlers' and 'land-crabs.'

title: Thief-Takers and the Law: Charlies, Bow Street Runners, and Redbreasts
summary: Pre-modern policing in Georgian London from Grose: the aged parish Charlies, the elite Bow Street Runners, scarlet redbreasts, and corrupt thief-takers.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.The Charlies: Decrepit, elderly parish night watchmen armed with lanterns and rattles; notorious for sleeping in their watchboxes or being tipped over.
quick_facts.Bow Street Runners: Founded by novelist Henry Fielding in 1749; London's first professional detective force; carried tipstaves with hollow crown heads.
quick_facts.Redbreasts / Traps: Slang for Bow Street Runners (derived from their signature scarlet red waistcoats worn under dark civilian coats).
quick_facts.Thief-Takers (Jonathan Wild): Private bounty hunters who captured thieves for legal rewards, but frequently ran the criminal syndicates themselves.

content:
The Primitive Dawn of Detection

Before Sir Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in 1829 ('Bobbies'), London had no unified professional police force. Public order was maintained by an unstable combination of corrupt parish watchmen, private thief-takers, and eight elite officers operating out of No. 4 Bow Street.

1. The Charlies (The Parish Watch)

Established under King Charles II. Elderly, poorly paid pensioners who patrolled the streets at night wearing heavy multi-caped coats, carrying an iron lantern and an oak rattle. Every half hour, they cried out the weather and time: 'Past two o'clock and a rainy morning!'
The Gentlemen's Sport: Aristocratic Regency bucks made a sport of getting drunk and 'boxing a Charlie'—creeping up behind the wooden watchbox while the old watchman slept inside and flipping the box face-down on the cobblestones, trapping the Charlie inside like a turtle.

2. The Bow Street Runners ('The Redbreasts')

The elite investigative force of the British Empire. They did not patrol beats; they investigated murders, highway robberies, and high-value bank heists across the entire nation:

  • Visual Mark: Wore plain dark civilian coats, but underneath wore a distinctive **scarlet red woolen waistcoat**, earning them the street names **The Redbreasts** or **The Traps**.
  • The Tipstaff (Warrant of Authority): Carried a small, 6-inch baton made of ebony wood or brass topped with a hollow crown (**the tipstaff**). Unscrewing the crown revealed the official magistrate's arrest warrant.

3. Thief-Takers and Squealers

The dark underbelly of pre-police justice. The government offered massive statutory rewards (the 'blood money' of £40) for the conviction of a highwayman or burglar. Corrupt thief-takers (epitomized by Jonathan Wild) actively organized gangs of young boys to commit burglaries, and then turned around and **squealed** (informed) on them to collect the £40 reward, sending their own pawns to the gallows.
fiction_tips: • The Rattle Alarm: When a Charlie spotted a burglar, he swung a heavy wooden **cog-rattle** (the watchman's rattle) around its handle, creating an ear-splitting, clattering wooden crack that echoed down the street, alerting adjacent watchmen. • The Bow Street Tipstaff Reveal: A dramatic detective moment: the investigator confronts a suspect in a crowded tavern; when the suspect reaches for a pistol, the Runner reaches into his coat, pulls out his brass-crowned ebony tipstaff, and bangs it on the counter: 'Bow Street, my lad. You're my prisoner.' • Blood Money Tension: Highlight the moral rot of 'blood money': a suspect terrified that his own best friend or lover will frame him because the reward money on his head will feed their family for three years.

title: Regency Flash Patter and Street Idiom: Rum Coves, Queer Bits, and Bone
summary: The nuanced idiom of 19th-century London street argot: decoding 'Flash Patter', the polarity between 'Rum' (good) and 'Queer' (bad), and slang verbs.

quick_facts.Source Work: 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue by Captain Francis Grose (1811)
quick_facts.Flash Patter: The fashionable slang dialect adopted by thieves, pugilists, coachmen, and fashionable young aristocrats.
quick_facts.The Rum vs Queer Polarity: Rum = Fine, noble, excellent, genuine; Queer = Bad, defective, counterfeit, dangerous, sickly.
quick_facts.Bone (The Ultimate Verb): To arrest, seize, steal, or take ('The trap boned the thief in the cellar').
quick_facts.Gammon: Deceptive talk, flattery, or humbug designed to distract someone ('None of your gammon!').

content:
The Dialect of Regency Cool

By 1811, ancient 17th-century underworld cant had merged with horse-coaching slang, pugilistic jargon, and tavern banter into a sophisticated, rapid street dialect known as **Flash Patter**. Lord Byron proudly boasted of his fluency in Flash, and young Regency dandies paid prize-fighters to tutor them in street patter so they could sound worldly in fashionable clubs.

The Foundational Dialect Polarity: Rum vs Queer

In Regency slang, two four-letter words served as universal modifiers across the entire language:

  • Rum (Positive / Genuine / Superior): Originally derived from 'Rome' (meaning noble).
    • Rum Cove: A fine, handsome, clever, or generous gentleman.
    • Rum Mort: A beautiful, well-dressed lady.
    • Rum Gelt: True gold or genuine bank notes.
    • Rum Snooze: A deep, comfortable, peaceful night's sleep.
  • Queer (Negative / Defective / Counterfeit / Rotten):
    • Queer Cove: An ugly, treacherous, or bankrupt villain.
    • Queer Bit: A counterfeit coin or forged promissory note.
    • Queer Plumper: A clumsy, unconvincing lie.
    • To Look Queer: To look sickly, pale, or guilty under interrogation.

Essential Flash Verbs

  • Bone: To seize or take. A thief bones a gold watch; an officer bones the thief.
  • Douse: To extinguish or put out ('Douse the glim!' = put out the candle).
  • Stow: To cease or hold your tongue ('Stow your whids' = shut your mouth).
  • Gammon: To fool someone with smooth, deceptive sweet-talk ('He tried to gammon the beak with a cock-and-bull story').
fiction_tips: • Bypassing Modern Misunderstandings: Explain to readers that in 1811, 'queer' did not have sexual connotations; it meant counterfeit, suspicious, or broken. A 'queer screen' was a forged five-pound banknote. • The Rum Paradox: Remind readers that calling an antagonist a 'rum cove' in 1811 was high praise for his cunning and dress, not an insult. • The Cadence of Flash Dialogue: Layer Flash vocabulary into natural speech rhythm: 'Stow that gammon, you queer prigger! If the traps bone you with that wedge in your fob, you'll dance the Tyburn jig before Michaelmas!'

title: Roget's Philosophical Taxonomy of Human Thought and Ideas
summary: The master conceptual architecture developed by Dr. Peter Mark Roget (1852) classifying all human knowledge into six fundamental philosophical domains.

quick_facts.Source Work: Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases by Peter Mark Roget (1852)
quick_facts.The Philosophical Goal: Not merely a dictionary of synonyms, but a philosophical map of human consciousness and universal ideas.
quick_facts.The Six Primary Classes: I. Abstract Relations | II. Space | III. Matter | IV. Intellect | V. Volition | VI. Affections.
quick_facts.The Principle of Polarity: Concepts are arranged in dialectical opposing pairs: Existence vs Inexistence, Unity vs Division, Power vs Impotence.
quick_facts.Historical Background: Devised by Roget as a polymath physician, mathematician, and Secretary of the Royal Society.

content:
The Philosophical Architecture of Roget's Mind

Unlike alphabetical dictionaries that begin with arbitrary letters (A to Z), Dr. Peter Mark Roget spent decades constructing an ontological taxonomy of reality. He sought a system where any human thought, emotion, or physical observation could be traced from universal cosmic abstractions down to granular nuances of expression.

The Six Master Classes of Roget's Universe

  1. Class I: Abstract Relations: The metaphysical and mathematical framework of reality: Existence, Nonexistence, Similarity, Quantity, Degree, Time, Causation, Power, and Order.
  2. Class II: Space: Dimensions, spatial orientations, motion, and geometry: Extension, Distance, Form, Motion, Velocity, Quiescence, Direction, and Navigation.
  3. Class III: Matter: The tangible, sensory material world: Inorganic vs Organic Bodies, Fluid vs Solid States, Heat, Sound, Light, Color, Odor, and Taste.
  4. Class IV: Intellect (The Mind): The internal machinery of human thought:
    • Formation of Ideas: Judgment, Reasoning, Discovery, Belief, Skepticism, and Delusion.
    • Communication of Ideas: Language, Eloquence, Secrecy, Rhetoric, Metaphor, and Epistolary expression.
  5. Class V: Volition (The Will): Human intentionality and dynamic action: Individual Will, Choice, Resolution, Hesitation, Pursuit, Avoidance, Authority, Conflict, and Moral Duty.
  6. Class VI: Affections (The Soul & Emotions): Sentient emotional experience: Joy, Despair, Sympathy, Malice, Hope, Fear, Pride, Humility, Love, Hatred, Religion, and Devotion.

The Dialectical Law of Dualities

Roget structured his thesaurus around polar opposites (dual columns). In Roget's vision, an author cannot truly comprehend a concept like Courage without simultaneously exploring its structural antithesis: Cowardice, Timidity, and Rashness. Every conceptual entry sits directly opposite its philosophical foil.
fiction_tips: • Bypassing Cliche Synonyms: Use Roget's classification not to find a 'fancy synonym', but to explore related conceptual families. If your hero is experiencing Doubt (Class IV), Roget links doubt to Unbelief, Suspicion, Hesitation, Puzzlement, and Mental Fog, giving rich psychological shading. • Character Dialectics: Create compelling antagonist foils using Roget's polar opposites: an intensely active character driven by Volition / Resolution (Section V) contrasted against a character trapped in Quiescence / Fatalism. • Worldbuilding Tone: When writing fantasy grimoires or sci-fi planetary surveys, organizing fictional texts around Roget's six classes creates an authentic 19th-century intellectual aura.

title: The Lexicon of Volition: Will, Resolution, Obstinacy, and Vacillation
summary: Exploring the spectrum of human intentionality and determination in Roget's Class V: from unbending tenacity to paralyzing indecision.

quick_facts.Source Work: Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases (Class V: Volition) by Peter Mark Roget
quick_facts.Narrative Application: Determines protagonist drive, antagonist relentlessness, and scene pacing.

content:
The Anatomy of Dramatic Will (Class V)

Drama is the collision of opposed human wills. In Class V (Volition), Roget isolates the exact linguistic gradients that separate a hero with relentless purpose from an obsessive tyrant or a paralyzed Hamlet.

The Four Degrees of Determination

  1. Calm Resolution (#604): Purpose, determination, firmness, decision, resolve, grit, fortitude, steady aim. The character knows their course and executes it without bravado.
  2. Obstinacy & Pig-Headedness (#606): Tenacity curdled into stubborn blindness: pig-headedness, contumacy, headstrong obstinacy, intractable, unyielding, dogged, recalcitrant, deaf to reason. This is the tragic flaw of kings and dogmatic leaders.
  3. Irresolution & Vacillation (#605): The internal battle that paralyzes action: shilly-shally, blowing hot and cold, wavering, hesitation, double-mindedness, dithering, pendulous indecision. Essential for moral suspense and ticking-clock scenes.
  4. Total Inertia (#683): Complete collapse of the motor drive: lethargy, torpor, passive fatalism, supineness, vegetative trance. Useful for post-trauma states or decadent ruling classes.

Authority, Resistance, and Subjugation

Volition also governs inter-personal dominance: Authority (#737) (sway, command, imperium, mastery) versus Subjection (#749) (bondage, vassalage, subservience, thrall) and Resistance (#719) (rebellion, defiance, insubordination, refusal).
fiction_tips: • Avoiding Static Dialogue: In high-stakes confrontation scenes, track the shift in volition. A character should not remain at 100% obstinacy; show the micro-vacillations (a sudden tremor in the throat, an unfinished sentence, an averted glance) before they re-anchor their resolve. • Antagonist Depth: Give your antagonist admirable Resolution rather than cartoonish evil; when an antagonist displays iron discipline, calm self-sacrifice, and unswerving focus, they become terrifyingly formidable. • The Climax Shift: The climax of almost every psychological novel occurs when a character transitions abruptly from Vacillation (#605) to irrevocable Resolution (#604).

title: Kinetic and Spatial Lexicons: Velocity, Navigation, and Dimension
summary: Mastering the sensory vocabulary of spatial dimensions, physical vectors, kinetic momentum, and stillness from Roget's Class II.

quick_facts.Source Work: Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases (Class II: Space) by Peter Mark Roget
quick_facts.Velocity Spectrum: Rapidity / Velocity (#274) vs Slowness (#275) vs Quiescence / Rest (#265).
quick_facts.Directional Vectors: Ascent (#305), Descent (#306), Circuitous Motion (#311), Convergence vs Divergence.
quick_facts.Action Pacing Utility: Provides granular, tactile verbs to replace repetitive action clichés.

content:
The Kinetic Engine of Roget's Class II

Class II (Space) provides the physical vocabulary necessary to ground readers in tangible reality and drive gripping action scenes without resorting to vague descriptions like 'he ran quickly' or 'the cave was huge.'

Kinetic Verbs of Velocity and Impact (#274)

Roget provides tiered verbs depending on the mass and mechanics of the moving body:

  • Darting / Projectile Speed: Bolt, dart, shoot, glance, streak, flit, ricochet, zip, scud, hurtle. (Ideal for arrows, shrapnel, small craft, or agile skirmishers).
  • Heavy / Crushing Momentum: Lumber, careen, plow, crash, trundle, thunder, plunge, surge, stampede. (Ideal for siege wagons, war galleys, cave-ins, or armored brutes).
  • Turbulent / Chaotic Motion (#315): Whirl, gyrate, eddy, buffet, churn, roil, heave, reel, convulse. (Essential for storms at sea, stampeding crowds, or hand-to-hand melees).

Spatial Geometry and Enclosure

Roget categorizes physical containment into contrasting atmospheres: Expansiveness (#194) (unbounded, cavernous, yawning, yawning chasm, limitless horizon) versus Narrowness & Confinement (#203, #229) (choked, claustrophobic, straitened, pinched, strangled passage, subterranean crevice).
fiction_tips: • The Pacing Accelerator: In high-speed chases, banish passive dimensional descriptions. Cut adjectives and stack monosyllabic kinetic verbs from Roget's Motion section: 'He ducked, vaulted the wall, hit the cobblestones, scrambled up, and bolted.' • The Sensory Transition: When moving a character from an open wilderness into a narrow cavern, consciously transition your vocabulary from Class II Expansiveness (vast, breezy, horizon) to Contraction (choked, damp, stooping, scraped shoulders) to trigger visceral reader empathy. • Directional Contrast: Compare a missile or arrow's straight, unyielding trajectory against a hunted animal's circuitous, zig-zagging flight.

title: The Spectrum of Human Affections: Sympathetic vs Malevolent Passions
summary: Psychological taxonomies of sentient emotion from Roget's Class VI: the polarity between altruistic sympathy and destructive malevolence.

quick_facts.Source Work: Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases (Class VI: Affections) by Peter Mark Roget
quick_facts.General Affections: Pleasure vs Pain, Joy vs Sorrow, Hope vs Despair, Pride vs Humility.
quick_facts.Sympathetic Passions: Benevolence, Tenderness, Pity, Forgiveness, Loyalty, Fraternal Love.
quick_facts.Malevolent Passions: Malevolence, Malice, Spite, Resentment, Vindictiveness, Cruelty, Jealousy, Contempt.
quick_facts.Subtle Emotional Shading: Distinguishing Envy (wanting what another has) from Jealousy (fearing loss of what you have).

content:
The Emotional Landscape of Class VI

Roget divided human emotion into moral, sympathetic, and self-regarding passions, offering fiction writers an exquisite spectrum of psychological depth:

1. The Dialectic of Sympathy (#906) vs Malevolence (#907)

  • Benevolence & Sympathy: Altruistic human connection: tender-heartedness, compassion, fellow-feeling, generosity, warm-heartedness, clemency, grace. In storytelling, sympathy is the binding glue that creates emotional reader investment.
  • Malevolence & Spite: The deliberate desire to inflict suffering: rancor, malice, venom, spite, ill-will, vindictiveness, bloodthirstiness. Real malevolence in literature is rarely cartoonish; it is rooted in wounded pride, perceived betrayal, or festering grievance.

2. The Complex Spectrum of Despair vs Hope

  • Hope (#858): The forward-looking virtue: anticipation, trust, optimism, promise, aspiration, sanguine expectation. Hope is fragile and dynamic.
  • Despair & Despondency (#859): The collapse of spiritual horizon: hopelessness, forlornness, resignation, bleakness, dejection, desolation, gloom. True despair in fiction is quiet; it manifests not as weeping, but as chilling emotional numbness and fatalistic surrender.

3. The Anatomy of Pride (#878) and Humiliation (#879)

Hubris (pride) precedes the tragic fall. Roget tracks pride through its many masks: haughtiness, arrogance, superciliousness, disdain, condescension, insolence, self-righteousness. Its foil is Humility: meekness, self-effacement, shame, abasement, modesty.
fiction_tips: • Layering Conflicted Emotions: Characters are most interesting when experiencing two opposing Roget affections simultaneously: a father who feels fierce Benevolence toward his daughter while harboring dark, simmering Resentment toward the husband she chose. • The Nuance of Malice: Give your villain's malice a specific flavor: is it cold, detached Superciliousness (contempt for inferiors), or is it boiling, feral Vindictiveness born of past humiliation? • Physical Manifestation: Connect Class VI Affections to physical involuntary body language: the dry throat, the cold sensation in the chest, the hollow ache in the solar plexus, the knuckles whitening against the table edge.

title: The Taxonomy of Matter: Textures, Odors, Sounds, and Sensation
summary: Mastering the sensory lexicon of the physical universe from Roget's Class III: acoustics, tactile states, luminescence, and pungent atmospheres.

quick_facts.Source Work: Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases (Class III: Matter) by Peter Mark Roget
quick_facts.Physical States: Inorganic vs Organic, Solid vs Fluid, Gaseous (#321-397).
quick_facts.Acoustic Spectra: Sound (#402), Resonance, Discord / Harsh Noise (#410), Silence (#403).

content:
The Tangible Universe of Class III

Great fiction relies on sensory immersion. Roget's Class III (Matter) systematically catalogues the physical qualities of substances and sensory impressions, providing authors with rich descriptive palettes.

1. Acoustic Nuances (#402–417)

  • Dull / Low-Frequency: Thud, boom, rumble, drone, groan, muffle, hollow thrum. (Heavy timber doors slamming, distant artillery, heartbeat in the ears).
  • Sharp / Piercing: Clink, clatter, rasp, snap, screak, ring, ping, shriek. (Blades parrying, ice cracking underfoot, glass splintering).
  • Subtle / Whispering: Rustle, murmur, sibilance, sigh, swish, lap, whisper. (Silk skirts brushing, dry leaves, gentle lake waves against cedar planks).

2. Tactile and Viscous States

Class III provides exact distinctions between textures: friable, brittle, gritty, greasy, gelatinous, viscid, slimy, ropy, ductile, malleable, spongy, corrugated, scabrous. Describing tactile resistance makes worldbuilding visceral.

3. Atmosphere, Odor, and Light

Roget distinguishes between Fragrance (#400) (balmy, aromatic, redolent, ambrosial) and Fetor (#401) (stifling, mephitic, foul, putrid, rancid, acrid, gamy). Pair odor with Luminescence (#420): scintillation, pallid shimmer, lurid glare, smoldering embers, lambent flame.
fiction_tips: • Sensory Triads: When introducing an evocative new location (a dungeon, an alchemist's lab, a Victorian engine room), evoke at least three distinct Class III senses: one acoustic, one tactile, and one olfactory. • Avoiding Cliché Lighting: Instead of 'the torch lit the room', explore Roget's lighting sub-classes: 'The resinous torch cast a smoky, lambent glare across the dripping granite, leaving deep pools of pitch in the vaulted corners.' • Tactile Verbs: Replace passive sensory descriptions with active tactile interactions: have characters run calloused thumbs over greasy copper or feel the crumbly friability of decayed plaster.

title: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations: Master Dramaturgical Architecture
summary: Georges Polti's foundational 1895 dramaturgical theory positing that all human storytelling reduces to 36 fundamental situational configurations.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations (Les Trente-six Situations Dramatiques) by Georges Polti (1895)
quick_facts.Philosophical Lineage: Built on the assertions of Carlo Gozzi and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.
quick_facts.Core Structural Principle: A situation is defined by dynamic relations between characters and fatal dilemmas, not by static settings or genres.
quick_facts.Dynamic Formula: Situation = Essential Characters + Central Crisis + Inevitable Relational Conflict.
quick_facts.Total Master Situations: Exactly 36 universal relational archetypes spanning vengeance, love, sacrifice, rivalry, and madness.

content:
The Dramaturgical Vision of Georges Polti

In 1895, French literary scholar Georges Polti took up a challenge initiated by Carlo Gozzi and affirmed by Goethe: the assertion that there can exist in drama and fiction only thirty-six distinct situational relationships. Polti analyzed over 1,200 plays, epic poems, classical tragedies, and contemporary novels to systematically catalogue and classify these 36 master archetypes.

Why Thirty-Six?

Polti discovered that drama does not arise from external events (a shipwreck, a battle, an inheritance), but from the emotional and moral tension generated between specific character archetypes locked in irreconcilable conflict. A situation requires an agonizing choice, a dynamic asymmetry of power, or a tragic clash between sacred duty and human passion.

Classification and Compound Plots

While amateur writers often view plots as linear chains of incidents, master storytellers construct novels by combining two or three Polti situations in sequence or counterpoint:

  • Main Plot / Subplot Harmony: A protagonist engaged in Situation IX: Daring Enterprise (a quest or heist) while dealing with a romantic subplot framed by Situation XXVIII: Obstacles to Love.
  • The Tragic Escalation: A character beginning in Situation I: Supplication, transitioning upon refusal into Situation VIII: Revolt, and culminating in Situation III: Crime Pursued by Vengeance.
fiction_tips: • Diagnosing Weak Second Acts: If your novel sags in the middle, identify the active Polti situation. A saggy middle usually means the relational dynamics have stabilized; introduce a secondary Polti situation (e.g. inject Situation XI: The Enigma or Situation XXIV: Rivalry of Superior and Inferior). • Genre Independence: The 36 situations apply equally to high fantasy, space opera, hard-boiled detective noir, and historical romance. A laser pistol and a bronze broadsword operate identically within Polti's framework. • Character Shifting: Increase dramatic tension by shifting a character's role within the same situation: an Avenger who realizes they have become the Criminal (Situation III).

title: Polti Situation 01: Supplication
summary: A powerless victim pleads for mercy or deliverance before a hesitant or hostile authority figure.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 01)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The Suppliant begs the Authority for protection from the Persecutor; or the Persecutor demands the surrender of the Suppliant from the Authority.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Persecutor; The Suppliant (pleader); The Power in Authority (arbiter).
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Priam begging Achilles for Hector's body; Esther pleading with Ahasuerus.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation I

Supplication is the quintessential opening gambit of tragedy. The core dynamic requires three distinct vertices: an unarmed, desperate Suppliant; an aggressive Persecutor who seeks their destruction; and a Power in Authority who possesses the sovereign might to protect the suppliant or cast them out.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Fugitives Imploring Powerful Aid: The suppliant arrives exhausted at a foreign court, demanding asylum against an invading emperor.
  2. Supplication of the Defeated: A conquered king or chieftain throws himself at the feet of the victor, begging not for his own life, but for the sparing of his children or citizens.
  3. Pleading for a Condemned Loved One: A spouse, parent, or child begs an unbending magistrate or judge to commute a death sentence before dawn.

Dramatic Friction Points

The scene's tension rests entirely upon the internal wavering of the Authority. If the Authority grants mercy immediately, the drama dissolves; if they refuse flatly without consideration, they become a cartoonish tyrant. The drama thrives in the Authority's agonizing calculation of political expediency versus moral conscience.
fiction_tips: • Strip Away Pride: Supplication is emotionally devastating when performed by a previously arrogant or stoic character. Show the physical toll: falling to the knees, trembling hands grasping the monarch's robe. • The Reluctant Arbiter: Give the Authority figure a legitimate, painful reason why granting mercy is dangerous or disastrous for their kingdom. • Sensory High-Stakes: Focus on the cold, echoing hall, the whisper of courtiers watching the humiliation, and the ticking clock of the executioner's bell.

title: Polti Situation 02: Deliverance
summary: An unfortunate victim trapped in fatal peril is rescued at the threshold of doom by an unexpected protector.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 02)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The Unfortunate is defenseless; the Threatener holds total dominion; the Rescuer breaches defenses to deliver them.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Unfortunate (captive/victim); The Threatener; The Rescuer.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Perseus rescuing Andromeda; Lancelot rescuing Guinevere from the stake.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation II

Deliverance is the cornerstone archetype of adventure and romance. Unlike mere physical escape, true Deliverance requires the arrival of an external force—the Rescuer—to break an otherwise inescapable doom imposed by the Threatener upon the helpless Unfortunate.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Rescue from Immediate Execution: The noose is around the hero's neck or the stake is smoldering when the rescuer charges the scaffold.
  2. Rescue of an Abandoned Innocent: Finding an infant left exposed in the wilderness or a prisoner locked in an oubliette.
  3. Unexpected Ally in Combat: A beleaguered warrior about to be overwhelmed by superior numbers is saved by the sudden arrival of an estranged comrade.

The Price of Deliverance

Polti emphasizes that high-caliber storytelling exacts a steep cost for deliverance: the rescuer often sustains mortal wounds, exhausts vital resources, or incurs a terrible moral debt to accomplish the extraction.
fiction_tips: • Earn the Rescue: Avoid the 'Deus ex Machina.' The Rescuer's arrival must be set up chapters in advance, with their timing governed by grueling physical effort. • The Psychological Aftermath: Being rescued does not instantly heal trauma; depict the survivor's disorientation, survivor's guilt, or complicated resentment toward their savior. • Ticking Clocks: Tighten pacing by syncing the Rescuer's progress with the Threatener's irreversible preparations (e.g. the lighting of the pyre).

title: Polti Situation 03: Crime Pursued by Vengeance
summary: An unpunished atrocity triggers an unrelenting avenger to pursue and destroy the perpetrator across all boundaries.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 03)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: A heinous transgression goes unpunished by legal institutions; the Avenger dedicates their existence to retribution.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Criminal; The Avenger; The Crime.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: The Count of Monte Cristo; The Bride in Kill Bill; Michael Kohlhaas.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation III

Situation III is the engine of revenge tragedy and legal thriller alike. When the institutional mechanisms of law fail to penalize a catastrophic violation, the Avenger assumes the mantle of cosmic justice, hunting the Criminal with monomaniacal focus.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Long-Deferred Vengeance: Decades pass while the avenger amasses wealth, skills, and intelligence to dismantle the criminal's empire piece by piece.
  2. Vengeance Against an Entire Class or Syndicate: The avenger systematically eliminates every co-conspirator who signed a death warrant.
  3. Vengeance Consuming the Avenger: In pursuing retribution, the avenger transforms into a monster far crueler than the original criminal.

Moral Ambiguity

The drama achieves greatness when the Criminal has genuinely repented, built a benevolent new life, or become a beloved public benefactor, forcing the audience to question whether vengeance is justice or senseless cruelty.
fiction_tips: • The Void of Fulfilment: When the final blow falls, do not write a triumphant hero. Show the chilling emptiness, the profound exhaustion, and the realization that blood does not resurrect the dead. • The Clever Trap: Great avengers do not merely stab their enemy; they orchestrate poetic retributions where the criminal is undone by their own defining vice (greed, paranoia, pride). • Collateral Damage: Force the Avenger to confront the innocent bystanders harmed by their relentless vendetta.

title: Polti Situation 04: Vengeance of a Kinsman upon a Kinsman
summary: A blood relation must be avenged, but the murderer is another member of the same family, tearing the avenger between filial piety and blood loyalty.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 04)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Sacred duty demands blood for blood, yet kinship prohibits spilling family blood (the ancient curse of kin-slaying).
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Slain Kinsman; The Guilty Kinsman; The Avenging Relative.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: The Oresteia (Orestes slaying Clytemnestra for Agamemnon); Hamlet avenging his father upon his uncle.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation IV

Situation IV represents one of the most agonizing paradoxes in classical and Renaissance dramaturgy. It elevates Situation III into mythic tragedy because the Avenger cannot strike down the Guilty Kinsman without committing the sacred sin of patricide, fratricide, or kin-slaying.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Avenging a Father upon a Mother: Orestes' classic dilemma—to avenge his royal father, he must spill the blood of the woman who birthed him.
  2. Avenging a Brother upon an Uncle: Hamlet's existential crisis—unmasking and slaying the king who is his mother's husband and his own bloodkin.
  3. Vengeance across Generational Feuds: Sibling turning upon sibling to fulfill an ancient ancestral blood oath.

Psychological Cost

The avenger is doomed regardless of their choice: inaction brands them a coward who betrays the dead, while action stains their soul with hereditary bloodguilt, often culminating in madness or self-destruction.
fiction_tips: • Physical Resemblance: Highlight the uncanny physical resemblance between the victim and the murderer—a shared jawline, identical voice, or inherited heirloom ring. • The Hesitation Moment: The climax should hang on a breathless hesitation where the avenger looks into eyes that mirror their own. • Supernatural Weight: Invoke ancestral curses, ghostly mandates, or religious taboos to heighten the pressure bearing down upon the young avenger.

title: Polti Situation 05: Pursuit
summary: A hunted fugitive flees across hostile territory while an unrelenting pursuer closes the distance.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 05)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: A desperate struggle of evasion, stamina, terrain utilization, and psychological warfare between hunter and prey.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Fugitive; The Pursuer.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Les Misérables (Javert hunting Jean Valjean); The Fugitive; No Country for Old Men.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation V

Situation V strips narrative down to kinetic adrenaline and spatial tension. The Fugitive is typically condemned by an unjust law, an oppressive regime, or a past mistake, while the Pursuer embodies relentless, bureaucratic, or instinctual tenacity.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Fugitive Fleeing for Innocence: Framed for a capital crime, the protagonist must evade both the law and the real killers while seeking proof.
  2. The Ideological Bloodhound: The pursuer is not evil, but fanatically moral—a lawman who believes that allowing even one rule to bend will unravel civilization.
  3. Prey Turning the Tables: The fugitive leads the hunter into deep wilderness or a labyrinth, transforming from prey into ambush predator.

Pacing and Geography

The landscape itself becomes an active third character: roaring rivers, treacherous mountain passes, sewer systems, and crowded bazaars dictate the physical parameters of the chase.
fiction_tips: • Track the Physical Toll: Don't let your fugitive run endlessly without cost. Show bleeding heels, infected scrapes, sleep deprivation, shivering from cold rain, and gnawing hunger. • The Respect of the Hunter: Deepen the relationship by having the pursuer study the fugitive's mind until they possess an intimate, almost erotic understanding of their habits. • Micro-Escapes: Structure the pursuit as a series of narrow, inventive escapes where each close call costs the fugitive an essential tool or ally.

title: Polti Situation 06: Disaster
summary: The catastrophic collapse of a ruling power, royal house, or city-state under the weight of invasion, pestilence, or natural fury.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 06)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Total ruin; the unraveling of centuries of civilization, glory, and security in a matter of hours or days.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Defeated Power; The Victorious Adversary (or Cataclysmic Nature).
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: The Fall of Troy; The Fall of the House of Usher; King Lear; The Fall of Constantinople.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation VI

Disaster is the spectacle of monumental fall from grace. Polti notes that Situation VI is distinct from mere misfortune because of its scale: it requires the overthrow of an empire, dynasty, or great fortress that previously seemed unshakeable.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Military Annihilation: The breach of the capital's outer walls, the sacking of palaces, and the burning of royal libraries.
  2. Dynastic Collapse: The hereditary madness or rot within a noble house that causes its towers to crumble both metaphorically and physically.
  3. Elemental Cataclysm: The volcanic eruption, flood, or virulent plague that sweeps away prince and peasant with cold, impartial finality.

Emotional Resonance: The Elegiac Tone

The emotional core of Situation VI is not panic, but profound melancholy—watching the golden statues topple into the mud and realizing that the era of greatness is ended forever.
fiction_tips: • The Contrast of Detail: Do not describe the burning city in generic terms. Ground the catastrophe in small, heartbreaking vignettes: an abandoned lute crushed under a soldier's boot, an unfinished feast covered in gray ash. • The Delusion of Safety: Open the scene with characters celebrating their impregnability just hours before the foundation stones give way. • The Sole Survivor: Frame the disaster through an observer who must carry the bitter memory of lost glory into a dark age.

title: Polti Situation 07: Falling Prey to Cruelty or Misfortune
summary: An innocent or helpless victim is subjected to arbitrary cruelty, torture, or confinement by a sadistic or systemic oppressor.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 07)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The victim has no immediate power to fight back or escape; survival depends purely upon endurance, dignity, and spiritual defiance.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Innocent / Helpless Victim; The Tyrant / Oppressor.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Job in the ashes; The Count of Monte Cristo in the Chateau d'If; Uncle Tom's Cabin; One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation VII

Situation VII generates deep visceral reader empathy and moral indignation. The protagonist is completely disarmed and delivered into the hands of arbitrary malice. There is no sword fight, no clever escape tunnel ready; there is only suffering and the struggle to preserve one's humanity.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Sadistic Jailer: A petty tyrant who abuses captive prisoners for personal amusement or bureaucratic power.
  2. Institutional Indifference: A vast, unfeeling system (workhouse, penal colony, insane asylum) that methodically crushes the individual spirit.
  3. Innocence in Chains: A gentle child or ascetic philosopher subjected to public humiliation and torment by a howling mob.

The Moral Core: The Unbroken Spirit

The dramatic victory in Situation VII is internal. The tyrant may break the protagonist's bones or tear their flesh, but fails utterly to extract the confession, submission, or loss of self-respect they demand.
fiction_tips: • Avoid Pure Sadism: Ensure the cruelty serves a thematic or psychological function. Give the oppressor an unsettling rationale—they genuinely believe they are 'reforming' the victim or maintaining divine order. • Small Acts of Resistance: Survival stories thrive on microscopic defiance: concealing a carved wooden token, sharing a dry crust of bread in the dark, or refusing to lower one's eyes. • The Physical Reality of Pain: Ground torment in realistic physiological reactions—cold sweat, hyperventilation, shock tremors, and the dissociation of the mind from the abused body.

title: Polti Situation 08: Revolt
summary: Oppressed subjects organize a clandestine conspiracy, rise in armed rebellion, and overthrow a tyrannical ruler.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 08)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The asymmetric struggle between entrenched imperial power and a desperate, clandestine underground.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Tyrant; The Conspirator / Rebel Leader.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Spartacus; William Tell; Julius Caesar (Brutus and Cassius); Star Wars.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation VIII

Revolt is the natural dramaturgical answer to Situation VII. The long-suppressed rage of the victims coalesces into organized, dangerous conspiracy. The drama moves between candlelit conspiratorial cellars and explosive public insurrection.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Reluctant Rebel: A peaceful citizen or loyal soldier pushed beyond endurance by a final atrocity committed against their family.
  2. The Aristocratic Conspiracy: Senators or generals plotting the assassination of an unstable emperor to preserve the republic.
  3. The Slaves' Uprising: The raw, elemental explosion of disenfranchised laborers breaking their chains and marching on the villas.

The Flaws of Rebellion

Polti emphasizes that great dramatists examine the fatal vulnerabilities of revolts: factional infighting among rebel factions, the ever-present threat of informants selling out the conspiracy, and the grim risk that the rebel leader will become the next tyrant.
fiction_tips: • The Paranoia of the Conspirators: Portray the grueling psychological toll of secrecy: every knock on the door sounds like the secret police; every comrade's sudden wealth looks like thirty pieces of silver. • The Tyrant's Perspective: Give the Tyrant genuine strategic arguments—they maintain peace, prevent savage barbarian invasions, or ensure food supplies, which the rebels' chaos will destroy. • The Tipping Point: Stage the precise moment where fear vanishes and the crowd realizes their collective strength: a single soldier refusing to fire on an old woman.

title: Polti Situation 09: Daring Enterprise
summary: A bold adventurer undertakes an ostensibly impossible physical, military, or logistical quest against overwhelming odds.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 09)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Audacity, specialized expertise, and relentless courage pitted against lethal natural or military defenses.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Bold Leader; The Difficult Object / Goal; The Adversary / Guardian.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Jason seeking the Golden Fleece; Hercules' Labors; The Guns of Navarone; Ocean's Eleven; The Lord of the Rings.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation IX

Situation IX is the engine of quest romance, epic fantasy, and heist fiction. The goal is clearly defined and widely acknowledged as suicidal or unattainable: stealing the dragon's hoard, penetrating the fortress vault, or planting explosives on the mountain guns.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Infiltration Heist: Bypassing magical wards, tripwires, guards, and locks using cunning, specialized tools, and precise timing.
  2. The Military Sortie: A tiny vanguard holding a narrow pass or making a daring raid behind enemy lines to destroy a siege engine.
  3. The Mythic Quest: Journeying into unexplored underworlds or uncharted ocean wastes to retrieve the only talisman capable of healing a dying land.

The Gathering of Specialists

A hallmark of Situation IX is the recruitment of distinct archetypes: the master locksmith, the demolitionist, the disgraced veteran, the cartographer, and the berserker, each whose unique flaw threatens the mission.
fiction_tips: • The Plan Must Fail: In storytelling, an enterprise where the original plan works smoothly is boring. Let the plan collapse at step two, forcing the characters to improvise under fire. • Tactile Preparations: Devote narrative time to the specialized gear: grappling hooks, oiled hinges, forged documents, specialized toxins, and secret maps. • Raise the Stakes: Ensure failure doesn't just mean death for the infiltrators, but the collapse of their civilization or the slaughter of their loved ones.

title: Polti Situation 10: Abduction
summary: The forcible seizure and carrying off of a prized person against their will, igniting an international conflict or family vendetta.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 10)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Violation of sovereignty and domestic sanctuary; the catalyst that unleashes armies and vendettas.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Abductor; The Abducted; The Guardian / Bereaved.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: The Abduction of Helen of Troy; The Rape of the Sabine Women; Taken; The Searchers.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation X

Abduction is one of the most volatile inciting incidents in world literature. It violates the sacred sanctity of home, marriage, or treaties, transforming the Guardian into an avenging warrior and the Abductor into the target of relentless pursuit.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Political Hostage: Kidnapping a prince or ambassador's daughter to extort concessions, land, or treaties from an empire.
  2. The Romantic / Mythic Kidnapping: A warlord or deity carrying off a mortal beauty into their fortress or underworld realm.
  3. The Child Stolen for Revenge: An old enemy snatching the heir of a king to raise them in squalor or train them to slay their own father.

The Agency of the Abducted

Modern narratives gain depth by granting the Abducted active internal agency: leaving clues along the trail, manipulating the captor's psychological weaknesses, or organizing an internal mutiny within the captor's stronghold.
fiction_tips: • The Chaos of the Snatch: Make the abduction scene chaotic, sudden, and terrifying—broken lanterns, shouting in the dark, the clatter of retreating hooves, and a discarded ribbon left on the stones. • The Guardian's Agony: Portray the horrifying guilt of the Guardian who stepped away for five minutes or trusted the wrong guard at the gate. • Captor-Captive Dynamics: Explore the psychological tension between the abductor and victim: fear, contempt, reluctant fascination, and ruthless bargaining.

title: Polti Situation 11: The Enigma
summary: A seemingly insoluble mystery, bizarre murder, or lethal riddle must be deciphered before disaster strikes.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 11)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: An intellectual battle between cunning deception and inductive forensic deduction under the pressure of mortal peril.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Questioner / Examiner; The Seeker / Detective; The Mystery / Riddle.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Oedipus and the Sphinx; Sherlock Holmes (A Study in Scarlet); The Name of the Rose; Knives Out.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XI

Situation XI is the classical foundation of detective fiction, courtroom drama, and riddle myths. A horrifying anomaly exists (a corpse inside a locked room, a Sphinx devouring travelers, a coded prophecy), and only pure intellect and observation can avert destruction.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Lethal Riddle: Answer correctly and gain a kingdom; answer wrongly and lose your head (e.g. Oedipus, Turandot).
  2. The Baffling Crime: A murder committed under impossible conditions where everyone has an alibi and the physical clues contradict physical laws.
  3. The Historical or Esoteric Secret: Decoding an ancient text or cipher to locate a hidden treasure before a ruthless rival cult reaches it.

The Fairness Principle

The greatness of Situation XI hinges on intellectual fairness: the clues must be visible to the audience, but woven so seamlessly into atmospheric background detail that their true significance is recognized only upon the final revelation.
fiction_tips: • The Red Herring with Emotional Weight: A false clue should not be arbitrary; it should reveal the secret, shameful vice or vulnerability of an innocent suspect. • The Physicality of Investigation: Ground the detective work in physical forensics: smelling ash for bitter almonds, examining ink drying times, measuring mud spatters on boot heels. • The Threat of the Clock: If the riddle isn't solved by moonrise or before the storm clears, the monster strikes again or the innocent suspect hangs.

title: Polti Situation 12: Obtaining
summary: Rival forces engage in a vicious diplomatic, commercial, or physical struggle to obtain a singular, irreplaceable prize.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 12)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Greed, ambition, and ruthless competition focused on a single scarce resource, talisman, or legal title.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Seeker; The Possessor / Rival; The Coveted Object.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: The Quest for the Holy Grail; The Maltese Falcon; Treasure Island; The Treasure of the Sierra Madre.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XII

Unlike Situation IX (where the focus is on the physical hazard of the enterprise), Situation XII focuses on the moral and tactical conflict between rivals contending for the same prize. The prize may be a sacred relic, a treasure map, a corporate monopoly, or a royal patent.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Treacherous Alliance: Rivals agree to cooperate to extract the prize from an impregnable vault, with each planning to slaughter the other the moment it is secured.
  2. The Bidding War: An escalating psychological duel fought in an auction house or diplomatic salon where fortunes and kingdoms are wagered.
  3. The Corrupting Relic: The prize exerts an insidious psychological influence, causing honorable comrades to murder each other for ownership.

The Irony of Possession

In Polti's most enduring examples, obtaining the prize brings not happiness, but ruin: the chest contains lead, the gold is cursed, or the prize is lost overboard during the final bloody duel.
fiction_tips: • Define the Irreplaceable Value: Make crystal clear why this object cannot simply be bought elsewhere or replicated. What transcendent power or absolute proof does it convey? • The Degradation of Morals: Show the gradual erosion of the protagonist's ethical red lines as the prize comes within arm's reach. • The Physical Object: Describe the weight, patina, cold metal feel, or antique scent of the coveted artifact to make the reader covet it too.

title: Polti Situation 13: Enmity of Kinsmen
summary: Brothers or close blood relations harbor visceral, hereditary hatred toward each other, erupting into murderous civil strife.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 13)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The bitterest hatred is that which springs from corrupted love and shared blood; domestic intimacy turned into savage warfare.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Malicious Kinsman; The Hated / Targeted Kinsman.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Cain and Abel; Eteocles and Polynices (The Thebaid); The Lion in Winter; Richard III; The Godfather Part II.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XIII

Situation XIII explores the terrifying reality that no enemy is more ruthless than a brother. Because siblings share childhood memories, inheritances, and intimate knowledge of each other's secret weaknesses, their warfare is devoid of chivalry.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Disinherited Brother: A younger or illegitimate son denied birthright and title, plotting the horrific destruction of the favored heir.
  2. Divided Sovereignty: Two brothers who inherit joint rule over a kingdom and immediately mobilize opposing armies to slaughter each other.
  3. The Parental Wedge: A manipulative father or mother who pits their children against one another in a sadistic competition for affection and wealth.

The Tragedy of Knowledge

In battle, stranger-enemies exchange blows blindly; brother-enemies strike at the precise psychological wound inflicted twenty years earlier in the nursery.
fiction_tips: • Weaponized Intimacy: Have the malicious brother use an intimate childhood secret or pet name as a mocking taunt right before springing the ambush. • The Trapped Family: Show the agony of mothers, sisters, and servants caught between two warring brothers whom they love equally. • The Inevitable Mutual Destruction: Polti notes that in classical myth, brothers locked in Situation XIII almost always perish on each other's swords simultaneously.

title: Polti Situation 14: Rivalry of Kinsmen
summary: Two close kinsmen become romantic or political rivals for the same lover, throne, or legacy, testing blood ties to the breaking point.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 14)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Competitive jealousy between equals sharing the same household; the slow poisoning of fraternal bonds.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Preferred Kinsman; The Rejected Kinsman; The Object of Rivalry.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Jacob and Esau; The Brothers Karamazov; King Lear (Goneril and Regan for Edmund).

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XIV

While Situation XIII deals with outright murderous hatred, Situation XIV focuses on the corrosive process of rivalry: two brothers or cousins who may genuinely love each other, but find their affections warped by competing for the same woman, inheritance, or royal favor.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Brothers Courting the Same Woman: One brother is chosen, leaving the rejected brother to smile at the wedding while bile burns his throat.
  2. The Deathbed Inheritance: Sons gathering around an expiring patriarch's bed, watching the notary's pen with predatory vigilance.
  3. The Younger Brother Outshining the Elder: A brilliant younger sibling whose military triumphs humiliate an insecure, legitimate elder brother.

The Escalation Ladder

The dramatic beauty of Situation XIV lies in its plausible escalation: starting with polite family dinners and passive-aggressive toasts, escalating through sabotage, and culminating in drawing steel behind the stables.
fiction_tips: • The Object's Agony: If the rivalry is romantic, give the contested person genuine moral horror at being the wedge tearing two brothers apart. • Childhood Flashbacks: Contrast the current bitter rivalry against a brief, touching memory of them defending each other against bullies as boys. • The Point of No Return: Mark the precise line that, once crossed (a forged letter, a poisoned hound, a stolen seal), destroys the brotherhood forever.

title: Polti Situation 15: Murderous Adultery
summary: Two adulterous lovers conspire to assassinate the inconvenient spouse who stands between them and total union.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 15)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: Illicit sexual passion weaponized into cold-blooded murder; domestic sanctuary turned into a slaughterhouse.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Adulterer; The Adulteress; The Betrayed Spouse.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Clytemnestra and Aegisthus slaying Agamemnon; Thérèse Raquin; Double Indemnity; The Postman Always Rings Twice.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XV

Situation XV is the engine of classic noir and classical royal tragedy. Sexual infatuation curdles into homicidal conspiracy. The betrayed spouse is an intolerable obstacle whose daily presence in the marriage bed becomes an affront to the lovers' delusion of romance.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. The Regicide Lovers: The queen and her paramour plotting to poison the king's goblet during his triumphant victory banquet.
  2. The Staged Accident: Modern noir—planning the staged drowned car, fake hunting mishap, or lethal insulin overdose to collect insurance.
  3. The Cowardly Seducer: The paramour convinces the desperate wife to administer the poison, intending to blackmail or abandon her once the husband is dead.

The Paranoid Hangover

The defining psychological insight of Situation XV is that murdering the spouse does not bring idyllic bliss. Once the deed is done, the lovers stare at each other with sudden, chilling terror: If you could kill them for me, when will you kill me for someone else?
fiction_tips: • The Intimacy of the Crime: The horror comes from familiarity—handing the husband his favorite hot soup laced with arsenic, or buttoning his coat before the rigged carriage ride. • The Unraveling Conspiracy: Show how minor domestic accidents (a barking dog, a forgotten handkerchief, a gossiping kitchen maid) ruin the 'perfect' murder. • Mutual Revulsion: After the funeral, show the physical revulsion that replaces their lust; touching each other now feels like touching the corpse.

title: Polti Situation 16: Madness
summary: A protagonist is seized by uncontrollable madness, delirium, or paranoia, committing horrific acts against their own loved ones in a psychotic fog.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 16)
quick_facts.Essential Dynamic: The betrayal of reality by one's own mind; committing atrocities while believing oneself to be saving the world or defending against monsters.
quick_facts.Essential Characters: The Madman; The Victim of the Madness.
quick_facts.Archetypal Examples: Hercules Furens (slaying his wife and children in madness); King Lear on the heath; The Shining (Jack Torrance); Shutter Island.

content:
Dramaturgical Anatomy of Situation XVI

Situation XVI is among the most terrifying configurations in literature because the antagonist resides inside the protagonist's own cranium. The horror does not stem from malevolence, but from tragic misperception—slaying a child while hallucinating a venomous serpent.

Key Variations and Sub-Classes

  1. Divine or Chemical Delirium: Slaying comrades or family under the influence of an alchemical draught, ancient curse, or psychotic fever.
  2. The Descent into Paranoia: A brilliant leader who begins seeing treason in every glance, systematically purging their most loyal friends.
  3. The Lucid Agony of the Madman: The tragic hero experiences brief, shattering moments of lucidity where they recognize their own decay and the blood on their hands.

The Awakening of Grief

The dramatic climax of Situation XVI is the terrifying return of sanity: the fog clears, the hallucinations dissolve, and the protagonist looks down to see the mangled bodies of those they loved more than life itself.
fiction_tips: • Subjective Reality: Write the scene strictly from inside the madman's sensory logic. To them, the sword blows are righteous, the victim's screams sound like demonic hisses, and the blood looks like spilled wine. • The Pre-Madness Symptoms: Plant early warning signs: insomnia, hyper-fixation on meaningless geometric patterns, auditory halos, and sudden irrational rages. • The Heartbreak of the Caretaker: Show the bewildered grief of the spouse or loyal knight who watches a great, noble mind rot into incoherence.

title: Polti Situation 17: Fatal Imprudence
summary: A thoughtless act of reckless curiosity, neglected duty, or arrogance unleashes irreversible catastrophe upon oneself and one's family.

quick_facts.Source Work: The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations by Georges Polti (Situation 17)
